result.outcome: The clinic operationalized the endoscopy plan by sending the colonoscopy referral. The patient moved into the endoscopy scheduling pathway.

observation.document_summary: Diagnostic colonoscopy was performed for intermittent BRBPR mixed with stool and thinner stools. The exam reached the cecum with excellent bowel preparation and found abnormal anterior distal rectal mucosa consistent with radiation proctitis or angiodysplasia, with no polyps or mass lesions; grade I internal hemorrhoids were also seen. The endoscopist prescribed sucralfate enemas and planned referral for APC treatment of radiation proctitis.

result.outcome: Colonoscopy clarified that the likely bleeding source was distal rectal radiation injury rather than colorectal neoplasia. Medical therapy with sucralfate enemas was started and referral for endoscopic ablation was initiated.

observation.document_summary: A prescription was issued for sucralfate enema therapy following colonoscopy findings of radiation proctitis. The order specified a 10% suspension, 20 mL per rectum twice daily for 14 days with two refills.

result.outcome: The patient received a defined topical treatment regimen for radiation proctitis while awaiting definitive endoscopic therapy.

observation.document_summary: The endoscopist formally referred the patient to gastroenterology for APC treatment of distal rectal radiation proctitis because APC equipment was not available at the original site. The referral included the prior colonoscopy report and noted a history of prostate cancer treated with radiation. A receiving office later indicated the initially targeted physician had no appointments due to upcoming maternity leave and asked that the referral be redirected.

result.outcome: A formal GI referral for APC was sent, but the first destination could not accommodate the patient. The case required redirection to another endoscopist capable of therapeutic sigmoidoscopy.

observation.document_summary: The patient called reporting ongoing bleeding and asking what to do because he was nearly finished the prescribed medication. Staff documented that refills had been faxed to the pharmacy and advised that he still needed to wait for gastroenterology to call with an appointment for flexible sigmoidoscopy treatment.

result.outcome: Symptom persistence was acknowledged, but the management plan remained medical therapy plus pending GI treatment. Medication access was maintained through refills.

observation.document_summary: Therapeutic flexible sigmoidoscopy was performed for rectal bleeding attributed to radiation proctitis after prior prostate cancer treatment. Pre-procedure information documented hemoglobin 120, platelets 227, WBC 5.3, INR 1.1, and normal electrolytes/creatinine. Severe radiation proctitis was found and treated with APC, with small to medium hemorrhoids also noted.

result.outcome: The patient underwent definitive endoscopic treatment of severe radiation proctitis with APC. A short-interval repeat therapeutic sigmoidoscopy was planned to assess response and retreat if needed.

observation.document_summary: After the APC treatment, the patient called asking whether he still needed to continue the daily sucralfate enema. The clinic documented that the enema no longer needed to be continued because he had received treatment for radiation proctitis and that the treating endoscopist planned another flexible sigmoidoscopy in 4 to 6 weeks.

result.outcome: Medical therapy was de-escalated after endoscopic treatment. The patient remained on the planned surveillance and retreatment pathway.

observation.document_summary: A repeat therapeutic flexible sigmoidoscopy was performed about six weeks later for known radiation proctitis. The report noted that the patient had responded well to the first APC treatment, with no rectal bleeding until the day of the procedure when bleeding likely reflected enema-related mucosal trauma. Endoscopy showed improved radiation proctitis, which was treated again using BiCap cautery, and medium internal grade II hemorrhoids were present.

result.outcome: The second therapeutic sigmoidoscopy confirmed improvement after initial APC and treated residual disease with BiCap cautery. Hemorrhoids remained present but were not identified as the main bleeding source.

observation.document_summary: Despite treatment of radiation proctitis, the family physician sent a new referral for consultation because the patient still had intermittent rectal bleeding and a recent sigmoidoscopy had shown internal hemorrhoids with advice to refer. The referral summarized the patient's history of radiation proctitis and listed comorbidities and active medications including Anusol products.

result.outcome: A new referral was generated to assess whether hemorrhoids were contributing to ongoing intermittent bleeding after treatment of radiation proctitis. The receiving clinic had not yet made a final management decision at this point.

observation.document_summary: The receiving specialist office acknowledged receipt of the referral and advised that the patient would be contacted closer to the triaged consultation date. The office also warned of prolonged COVID-related wait times, with hemorrhoid consultations expected to wait about three months and general consultation booking delays of four to six months.

result.outcome: The referral was accepted administratively into the queue, but no near-term consultation was offered. The patient remained in a delayed scheduling pathway.

observation.document_summary: An internal task reviewed the recent flexible sigmoidoscopy and concluded that the patient could be redirected back to the ambulatory endoscopy service rather than being seen in the receiving office. This suggests the clinic judged the ongoing issue to be better managed through the prior therapeutic endoscopy pathway than a new hemorrhoid consultation.

result.outcome: The receiving office chose not to proceed with consultation and instead redirected the patient back to the prior service. Management focus remained on the treated radiation proctitis pathway rather than standalone hemorrhoid care.
